paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can represent future rewards by their average, but that average leaves out how possible returns are distributed. This paper argues that learning the distribution itself matters for reinforcement learning more broadly, beyond specific uses such as choosing actions according to risk preferences.

The authors study this perspective theoretically in both policy evaluation and control. Policy evaluation assesses an existing policy, while control involves learning which actions to take. Their analysis identifies a significant distributional instability in the control setting. They also develop an algorithm that uses Bellman’s equation to learn approximate return distributions, turning the distributional viewpoint into a concrete learning method.

On games from the Arcade Learning Environment, the algorithm achieves results reported as state of the art. The authors combine these experiments with theory and anecdotal evidence to examine how return distributions affect approximate learning. The contribution therefore includes both a successful algorithm and an account of why distributional information can influence learning, alongside an identified theoretical difficulty in control.
icml-2017-a-distributional-perspective-o.tldr: Learning distributions of future returns yields a successful reinforcement learning algorithm while revealing distributional instability in control.

paragraphs: Clustering sensitive records requires balancing useful groupings with protection for the individuals represented in the data. This paper studies that problem in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where private clustering was less understood than in low-dimensional discrete settings. It develops efficient, differentially private algorithms for both k-means and k-median.

For dimensions at least on the order of a polylogarithmic function of the number of records, the algorithms provide improved clustering-loss guarantees. Their bound combines the optimal loss multiplied by log cubed of the dataset size with an additive term polynomial in the logarithm of that size, the dimension, and the number of clusters. The previous bound described in the abstract had a square-root dimension multiplier and an additive term involving dimension-dependent powers.

The authors also consider sparse records, where each point has only a limited number of nonzero coordinates. In that case, the additive bound depends polynomially on log dimension and sparsity. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the method’s effectiveness, complementing the theoretical improvements.
icml-2017-differentially-private-cluster.tldr: Efficient private clustering algorithms improve high-dimensional loss guarantees, with further dimension savings for sparse data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn discrete graphical models while preserving differential privacy. One option is to keep the entire learning procedure behind a privacy barrier. Another is to release protected summary statistics and then learn from those summaries. The authors find that adding Laplace noise to sufficient statistics offers a useful balance of privacy, model quality, and practicality.

Even a straightforward learner that accepts those noisy statistics directly outperforms general-purpose private learning algorithms in their study. However, the authors identify specific problems with that approach: it disregards information about how the data were generated, has uncertain theoretical foundations, and can exhibit pathological behavior. Noise-protected summaries therefore require care in how they are interpreted.

Their proposed solution uses collective graphical models to infer the underlying true sufficient statistics within an expectation-maximization procedure. This explicitly treats the released summaries as noisy observations rather than unquestioned inputs. Experiments on synthetic data and a human-mobility case study show that the resulting procedure learns better models than the competing approaches tested.
icml-2017-differentially-private-learnin.tldr: Inferring true sufficient statistics from privacy-protected noisy summaries improves graphical-model learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Words can change meaning over time, so a single fixed representation can conceal meaningful shifts. This paper introduces a probabilistic language model for text with timestamps. It represents both words and their contexts as trajectories through an embedding space, making semantic change part of the model itself.

At each time, the representations follow a probabilistic version of word2vec. A latent diffusion process connects these representations across time while allowing them to drift. This connection lets learning share information across the text collection instead of treating each time slice as a separate modeling problem. The authors describe two scalable variational inference algorithms, called skip-gram smoothing and skip-gram filtering, for training the temporal model.

Experiments on three corpora compare the approach with static models trained separately on time slices. The dynamic model produces trajectories reported as more interpretable and achieves higher predictive likelihoods. These findings support connecting representations through time as a way to capture semantic evolution while still using information distributed across the available text.
icml-2017-dynamic-word-embeddings-c596ed.tldr: A temporal word-embedding model tracks semantic change and improves interpretability and predictive likelihood over separately trained static models.

paragraphs: This paper addresses online multiclass prediction with bandit feedback, where learning proceeds over rounds with limited feedback about predictions. The central question is whether a computationally efficient algorithm can also achieve a strong regret guarantee. Regret measures accumulated predictive loss relative to a comparison benchmark, so its growth describes how the cost of learning builds up over time.

The authors introduce an efficient second-order algorithm with regret scaling as the square root of the number of rounds, multiplied by an inverse parameter factor and with logarithmic factors suppressed. The guarantee applies simultaneously across a parameterized family of losses that spans hinge loss through squared hinge loss. Because the displayed bound includes an inverse parameter, it does not provide a finite bound by directly substituting zero at the hinge-loss endpoint.

The result resolves the stated open problem concerning efficient square-root-regret bandit multiclass prediction. Experiments also show favorable performance against earlier algorithms. Together, the theoretical and empirical findings support the method’s computational and predictive usefulness within the studied setting.
icml-2017-efficient-online-bandit-multic.tldr: An efficient second-order algorithm achieves parameter-dependent square-root regret for online multiclass learning with bandit feedback.

paragraphs: A decision maker’s choices can reveal what they are trying to optimize, even when their objective is hidden. This paper studies how to learn that objective by observing problem inputs and the corresponding decisions over multiple rounds. The task reverses ordinary optimization: the observed solutions become evidence about the function that produced them.

The proposed framework uses online learning and applies to linear objectives over arbitrary feasible sets, provided a linear optimization oracle is available. That oracle supplies a way to optimize a linear function over the relevant set. This assumption gives the framework broad scope while identifying the computational capability it needs. The approach generalizes previous methods based on decomposing optimality conditions and using dual formulations.

The authors prove convergence at a rate proportional to one over the square root of the number of rounds. They also briefly discuss extending the framework to learn linear constraints. Preliminary computational results demonstrate effectiveness and applications, giving initial practical support to the objective-learning method and its theoretical analysis.
icml-2017-emulating-the-expert-inverse-o.tldr: Online learning recovers linear decision objectives from repeated observed choices when a suitable optimization oracle is available.

paragraphs: Adversarial imitation learning trains a policy using a discriminator that distinguishes its behavior from expert behavior. The paper addresses a difficulty that arises when a stochastic policy is used as the generator: the computation is no longer differentiable from end to end. Training then requires gradient estimates with high variance.

The authors introduce Model-based Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning, or MGAIL. Its central step is to incorporate a forward model that makes the computation fully differentiable. This allows policy training to use the exact gradient of the discriminator through that computation. The forward model therefore changes how the discriminator’s learning signal reaches the policy, addressing the gradient-estimation issue identified in the model-free setup.

The resulting algorithm learns competent policies with relatively fewer expert examples and interactions with the environment. The authors evaluate it in domains with both discrete and continuous actions and report results surpassing the state of the art. These findings support the proposed differentiable approach as a practical way to improve the efficiency of learning from expert behavior.
icml-2017-end-to-end-differentiable-adve.tldr: MGAIL uses a forward model to make adversarial imitation differentiable and reports stronger, more sample-efficient policy learning.

paragraphs: Structured Prediction Energy Networks assign an energy to each candidate structured output using a deep network. Prediction then searches for a low-energy output through gradient-based optimization. This paper develops end-to-end training that back-propagates through that prediction process, allowing the energy function to learn from the procedure used to produce predictions.

The authors report substantially better accuracy than the earlier structured SVM training method in their experience. They attribute this benefit to the ability to use more sophisticated non-convex energy functions. They also provide techniques to improve speed, accuracy, and memory requirements, addressing the practical costs of training through an optimization procedure.

The method is demonstrated on 7-Scenes image denoising and CoNLL-2005 semantic role labeling. In both tasks, approximate minimization of the richer non-convex energies outperforms baselines whose simpler energies can be minimized exactly. The findings show that, in these experiments, the expressive quality of the energy function matters enough to outweigh the advantage of exact optimization for a simpler model.
icml-2017-end-to-end-learning-for-struct.tldr: Training through prediction optimization lets structured energy networks use richer energies that outperform simpler, exactly optimized baselines on two tasks.

paragraphs: Ensembles of decision trees can require substantial memory, creating difficulties when resources are limited and affecting fitting and prediction time. This paper introduces the Globally Induced Forest, or GIF, to build lightweight tree ensembles under memory constraints. The objective is to retain accurate predictions while controlling the size of the model being constructed.

GIF uses a fast prepruning approach that iteratively deepens the current forest. Size control is therefore part of the construction process. The method combines local and global optimization, bringing both levels of consideration into how the forest grows. This combination is intended to produce accurate ensembles within a memory budget and in a reasonable amount of time.

The authors report that GIF is more than competitive with standard tree-based ensembles under corresponding resource constraints. In some cases, it even outperforms substantially larger models. These results support the value of coordinating forest growth when memory is limited, while the claim about surpassing larger ensembles remains explicitly dependent on the case.
icml-2017-globally-induced-forest-a-prep.tldr: Globally Induced Forest builds compact tree ensembles that compete strongly under memory constraints and sometimes outperform much larger models.

paragraphs: Greedy selection builds a set by repeatedly choosing an attractive next addition. It has strong guarantees for submodular objectives, which exhibit a diminishing-returns structure, but often also works well when that structure is absent. This paper develops guarantees for nondecreasing, non-submodular objectives when the number of selected items is constrained.

The analysis describes performance using two quantities: generalized curvature, alpha, and the submodularity ratio, gamma. Together they yield a tight approximation guarantee of (1 − exp(−gamma × alpha)) / alpha. This connects the strength of the greedy solution to measurable properties of the objective, providing a theoretical explanation for performance beyond the usual submodular setting.

The authors bound these quantities for several objectives, including Bayesian A-optimal experimental design, determinants of square submatrices, and certain linear programs with combinatorial constraints. Experiments on synthetic and real-world applications support the theoretical findings. The contribution gives objective-specific ways to assess greedy selection, with the guarantee depending on the curvature and submodularity ratio.
icml-2017-guarantees-for-greedy-maximiza.tldr: A tight guarantee explains greedy maximization for non-submodular objectives through their curvature and submodularity ratio.

paragraphs: The Viterbi algorithm finds the most likely hidden-state path explaining a sequence of observations in a Hidden Markov Model. With T observations and n states, its standard running time is O(Tn²). This paper investigates why obtaining substantially faster general algorithms has remained difficult despite sustained interest.

The authors establish matching conditional lower bounds. These rely on assumptions that the best known algorithms for All-Pairs Shortest Paths and maximum-weight k-clique are essentially optimal. The implication is conditional: major Viterbi improvements would also imply faster algorithms for those underlying problems. The results explain the obstacle through connections to other computational tasks without claiming an unconditional impossibility theorem.

The paper also identifies an opportunity when a model has few distinct transition probabilities. Using an online Boolean matrix-vector multiplication algorithm, the authors obtain a speedup factor of 2 raised to an order of square root log n. This special-case improvement shows how structure in transition probabilities can permit acceleration even while the general problem faces the stated conditional barriers.
icml-2017-improving-viterbi-is-hard-bett.tldr: Conditional lower bounds explain Viterbi’s resistance to speedups, while few distinct transition probabilities enable a faster special case.

paragraphs: Active learning involves choosing which items to obtain labels for, making the selection procedure part of the learning problem. This paper proposes learning that procedure through metalearning across a distribution of related tasks. Its focus is on developing an active learning algorithm whose components are learned together.

The model jointly learns a representation of the data, a heuristic for selecting items, and a function for making predictions. The selection heuristic constructs a labeled support set, which is then used to train the prediction function. These components form a connected process: the representation describes the items, selection determines the labeled evidence available, and prediction uses that evidence. Joint learning brings all three decisions into the same framework.

The authors test the model using Omniglot and MovieLens in both synthetic and practical settings. The stated contribution is the integrated metalearning approach and its evaluation across these settings. It treats deciding what to label as a capability that can itself be learned from related tasks, alongside how to represent data and make predictions.
icml-2017-learning-algorithms-for-active.tldr: A metalearning model jointly learns data representations, label-selection heuristics, and predictors across related tasks.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Periodic Spatial GAN, or PSGAN, for generating textures with a generative adversarial network. The method can learn multiple textures from datasets containing one or more complex large images. It handles both periodic textures, which repeat, and non-periodic textures, giving the same approach scope across different visual patterns.

A central result concerns the organization of the generator’s structured noise space. Moving smoothly between samples in that space produces new images that appear perceptually between textures in the training data. The authors describe this behavior as having the properties of a texture manifold. It means the learned representation supports transitions among textures as well as the generation of individual samples.

Multiple experiments demonstrate flexibility across diverse texture and image sources. The authors also report that the method scales well and can generate images of arbitrarily large size. Together, these capabilities support learning a collection of textures, exploring visual mixtures between them, and producing outputs whose size is not fixed to a single image dimension.
icml-2017-learning-texture-manifolds-wit.tldr: PSGAN learns diverse textures, smoothly interpolates between them, and supports generating arbitrarily large texture images.

paragraphs: Weak supervision sources can supply training labels at scale, but their dependencies affect the quality of labels inferred by a generative model. Choosing those dependencies is difficult when no labeled data are available to guide the choice. This paper proposes a way to estimate the model’s dependency structure using only unlabeled observations.

The method maximizes a marginal pseudolikelihood objective with l1 regularization, combining a structure-estimation criterion with a preference for sparsity. For a broad class of models, the authors show that the amount of unlabeled data needed to identify the true structure grows sublinearly with the number of possible dependencies. This gives a theoretical reason that examining a large space of dependencies need not require proportionally more data.

In simulations, the method is reported to be 100 times faster than a maximum-likelihood approach and to select one quarter as many extraneous dependencies. On real information-extraction applications, including PubMed abstracts, it improves existing user-developed systems by an average of 1.5 F1 points. These findings connect structure estimation to practical label quality.
icml-2017-learning-the-structure-of-gene.tldr: Sparse dependency estimation from unlabeled data improves generative weak-supervision models, with theoretical sample guarantees and practical gains.

paragraphs: Discovering the structure of an undirected graphical model from few observations is challenging. Common methods estimate a penalized precision matrix, so recovering edges follows indirectly from fitting the data. This paper explores learning edge discovery directly, especially when generating example datasets with desired graph properties may be easier than expressing those properties through penalties.

The authors train a neural network to map empirical covariance matrices to estimated graph structures. Synthetic training examples encode the kinds of structure and sparsity the model should recognize. Learning from them implicitly supplies structural preferences, while the training task can focus specifically on identifying edges instead of maximizing data likelihood.

The trained method generalizes to unseen synthetic and real datasets in the reported experiments. Results on genetics, brain imaging, and simulation data are generally superior to analytical methods. These findings support using generated examples to teach a graph-discovery procedure, with the empirical success extending beyond the particular data encountered during training and without implying superiority on every dataset.
icml-2017-learning-to-discover-sparse-gr.tldr: A neural network trained on synthetic graphs learns to infer edges from covariance matrices and generalizes well in reported real-data evaluations.

paragraphs: The Gumbel trick uses random perturbations and repeated most-likely-configuration searches to sample discrete distributions or estimate their normalizing partition functions. This paper shows that the trick belongs to a broader family of related methods. Several members have better properties in particular settings while adding little computational cost.

For discrete graphical models, perturbing every possible configuration can undermine the computational benefits of this approach. A common alternative uses low-rank perturbations. The authors show how a subfamily of their methods works in this setting, deriving new upper and lower bounds on the log partition function. They also construct a family of sequential samplers for the Gibbs distribution, extending the framework from normalization estimates to sampling.

The comparison remains qualified: the new methods improve on the Gumbel trick in several settings, while the original method retains advantages. In particular, its simpler analytical form enables additional theoretical results. The contribution broadens the set of perturbation-based tools and clarifies that their benefits depend on both computational and analytical considerations.
icml-2017-lost-relatives-of-the-gumbel-t.tldr: A broader family of Gumbel-related methods improves some sampling and normalization tasks while preserving useful tradeoffs with the original trick.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to explore efficiently in finite-horizon Markov decision processes. Exploration must gather information while limiting the rewards lost through imperfect decisions. The authors modify value iteration with optimism and prove a regret bound that improves on the previous bound attributed to UCRL2.

Writing H for the horizon, S for states, A for actions, and T for time steps, the bound is of order sqrt(HSAT) + H²S²A + H sqrt(T), apart from logarithmic factors. When T is at least H³S³A and SA is at least H, it simplifies to order sqrt(HSAT). In that regime it matches the established lower bound up to a logarithmic factor, giving a qualified optimality result.

Two analytical choices drive the improvement. The proof controls uncertainty in the optimal value function as a whole, improving state dependence. Bernstein-based exploration bonuses use empirical variance in estimated next-state values, improving horizon dependence. These choices connect the strength of exploration incentives to uncertainty in values and yield sharper guarantees.
icml-2017-minimax-regret-bounds-for-rein.tldr: Optimistic value iteration achieves regret matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors under stated horizon, size, and duration conditions.

paragraphs: This paper automates the search for optimization rules used to train deep networks. Instead of specifying a complete update equation by hand, the method learns to construct one from primitive ingredients. These ingredients include the current gradient and a running average of gradients, providing a vocabulary for describing candidate optimization methods.

A recurrent neural network controller generates a string in a domain-specific language that represents a mathematical update equation. Reinforcement learning trains the controller to maximize a model’s performance after a few training epochs. The search therefore evaluates proposed rules through their effect on training, linking the symbolic construction of an optimizer to observed model performance.

On a CIFAR-10 convolutional network, the approach discovers several rules that outperform commonly used optimizers, including Adam, RMSProp, and versions of stochastic gradient descent with and without momentum. The discovered optimizers also transfer successfully to other architectures, including Google’s neural machine translation system. These results support automated optimizer discovery and show useful transfer beyond the initial search setting.
icml-2017-neural-optimizer-search-with-r.tldr: A reinforcement-trained controller discovers optimizer equations that perform well on a convolutional network and transfer to other architectures.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks with rectifiers and max-pooling lack both smoothness and convexity, so standard optimization guarantees do not directly apply. Yet their training routinely uses methods drawn from convex optimization. This paper introduces neural Taylor approximations and an associated Taylor loss to analyze optimization in this setting.

The authors present a convergence guarantee applicable to modern convolutional networks and report that it matches a lower bound for convex nonsmooth functions. Taylor expansions provide the central analytical tool. Experiments spanning optimizers, network layers, and tasks offer evidence that the analysis captures the observed dynamics of neural optimization. The convergence statement should be understood within this analytical framework, without extending it to a claim of finding global optima.

The paper also uses the approximation to examine shattered gradients as a central training difficulty in rectifier networks. It investigates whether adaptive optimizers such as RMSProp and Adam reach better solutions by exploring activation configurations more thoroughly. This proposed explanation remains a hypothesis under investigation, alongside the paper’s convergence analysis and experimental evidence.
icml-2017-neural-taylor-approximations-c.tldr: Neural Taylor approximations support convergence analysis and investigate how activation exploration may help adaptive optimizers train rectifier networks.

paragraphs: Random Fourier features are widely used to make kernel methods more scalable, including kernel ridge regression. Their empirical success raises a theoretical question: how does replacing the kernel representation with random features affect the statistical behavior of the resulting learner? This paper takes steps toward answering that question through matrix approximation.

The authors study random Fourier features from a spectral perspective. This focuses on how well the feature-based matrix approximates the relevant kernel matrix in spectral terms. They derive tight bounds on the number of Fourier features required to achieve such an approximation. Feature count becomes a quantity tied to a mathematical approximation target, giving theoretical substance to the choice of representation size.

The paper then connects those matrix bounds to statistical guarantees for kernel ridge regression. This bridge matters because a good matrix approximation must ultimately support reliable learning behavior to justify its use. The contribution links the computational device of random features with statistical analysis, strengthening the theoretical account behind a technique already successful in practice.
icml-2017-random-fourier-features-for-ke.tldr: Tight spectral approximation bounds connect the number of random Fourier features to statistical guarantees for kernel ridge regression.

paragraphs: Learning a sequential model from one trajectory means working with observations that depend on one another. This differs from the classical assumption that multiple independent, identically distributed trajectories are available. The paper develops spectral methods of moments for this single-trajectory setting, addressing the dependence within the data directly in its analysis.

The approach builds on an efficient learning algorithm for weighted automata based on singular value decomposition. The authors state and analyze it across three increasingly difficult settings: probabilistic automata, stochastic weighted automata, and reactive predictive state representations controlled by a finite-state policy. This progression extends the analysis from sequential probabilistic models to a setting where a policy influences the observed process.

The proofs introduce tools for studying the mixing properties of stochastic weighted automata. These properties are relevant to understanding how dependence persists along a trajectory. The main contribution is a rigorous foundation for learning several important sequential model classes from dependent data, broadening the circumstances in which spectral learning can be justified.
icml-2017-spectral-learning-from-a-singl.tldr: Spectral methods learn sequential models from one dependent trajectory, with rigorous analysis extending to finite-state policy control.

paragraphs: When multiple learning agents interact, their individual updates need to fit together in a well-behaved way. This paper formalizes a notion of safety based on doing no harm and studies agents that change their actions using gradient descent. Its safety claims concern this mathematical interaction setting.

The authors show that gradient descent converges to a Nash equilibrium in safe games. Their main contribution is a definition of strongly-typed agents together with a proof that such agents interact safely. Strong typing thus supplies sufficient conditions for the desired behavior: satisfying those conditions provides a guarantee, without establishing that every safe interaction must have that form.

Examples connect strong typing to several existing ideas. It generalizes certain features of convexity, relates closely to blind source separation, and offers a tensor-decomposition perspective on classical multilinear games. These connections help explain the structure behind the guarantee. The paper’s contribution is a mathematical route from specified agent properties to safe interactions and convergence within the studied gradient-based framework.
icml-2017-strongly-typed-agents-are-guar.tldr: Strong typing provides sufficient conditions for safe gradient-based agent interactions, with convergence to Nash equilibrium in safe games.

paragraphs: Keeping gradients from vanishing or exploding does not fully explain why very deep networks can be difficult to train. This paper identifies another problem: gradients can lose their correlation as depth increases, eventually resembling white noise. The authors call this phenomenon gradient shattering and use it to investigate the advantages of skip connections.

Their analysis shows exponential decay of gradient correlations with depth in standard feedforward networks. Architectures with skip connections are more resistant, with sublinear decay. Empirical evidence from both fully connected networks and convolutional networks supports the analysis. This shifts attention from gradient magnitude alone to the structure of the gradients that guide learning.

The authors also introduce a looks-linear initialization designed to prevent shattering. Preliminary experiments show that this initialization allows very deep networks to be trained without adding skip connections. Those early results suggest initialization can address the identified problem, while the broader contribution explains an optimization difficulty that remains relevant even when gradient magnitudes are well controlled.
icml-2017-the-shattered-gradients-proble.tldr: Gradient correlations can shatter with depth; skip connections resist this effect, and a new initialization shows preliminary promise in preventing it.

paragraphs: A clustering solution’s loss on a sample can differ from its expected loss on the underlying population. Uniform deviation bounds control this difference across all candidate models at once. This paper develops a framework for obtaining such guarantees when the loss is unbounded, then applies it to k-means clustering under weak distributional assumptions.

If the underlying distribution has a bounded fourth moment, the authors prove a deviation rate of O(m to the power −1/2), improving on the previously known O(m to the power −1/4), where m is sample size. The faster rate means the guaranteed discrepancy shrinks more quickly as additional observations become available. The analysis also makes the dependence on kurtosis explicit, connecting the guarantee to the distribution’s tail behavior.

The paper provides further improved rates under stronger assumptions, including bounded higher moments, subgaussianity, and bounded support. These results organize the guarantees around properties of the data distribution. They show how stronger control of extreme observations can support sharper connections between sample clustering loss and expected loss.
icml-2017-uniform-deviation-bounds-for-k.tldr: A framework for unbounded losses sharpens k-means generalization guarantees, with rates governed by moment and tail assumptions.

paragraphs: Ordinal classification predicts categories that have a meaningful order. A model produces probabilities over those categories, so the shape of that distribution is part of its output. This paper observes that distributions learned with cross-entropy can have undesirable properties for ordinal problems and proposes explicitly constraining their shape.

The proposed technique uses Poisson and binomial probability distributions to make the discrete ordinal predictions unimodal. Unimodality means the probabilities form a single peak across the ordered categories. This imposes structure on how probability is distributed across possible answers, going beyond merely producing a probability for each category. The authors present the technique as a straightforward way to incorporate this requirement into deep ordinal classification.

The approach is evaluated on two large ordinal image datasets, with results described as promising. The stated finding supports further use of the proposed distributional constraint in this setting. The contribution centers on making an intended property of ordinal predictions explicit in their probability distributions and demonstrating the approach in deep learning experiments.
icml-2017-unimodal-probability-distribut.tldr: Poisson and binomial constructions enforce unimodal predictions for deep ordinal classification, with promising results on two image datasets.
